messages.author: 77e72e34bf8c033f
messages.subject: Performance penalty using truncated priors?
parts:
Hi all

I am working with additive models where I frequently need to constrain the sign of the fitting coefficient, e.g.

y = a * x1 + b * x2 + c * x3

say I want a to be positive and have a decreasing prior for large values. I typically do this using one of these priors

a ~ normal(0, 50) T[0.0,];

or 

a ~ gamma(1, 0.025);

where I define 

real<lower=0> a;

in both cases. 

My question is whether I suffer in performance, using the truncated normal distribution compared to the inherently positive gamma distribution?

Thanks in advance,
Per

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Performance penalty using truncated priors?
parts:
Hi Per,

I'll start by answering your question:
No, you will not suffer in computational performance by using the
truncated normal distribution, or any other distribution.

If you declare `a` as a parameter:
real<lower=0> a;

Truncating the prior is computationally worse. Instead of

use
a ~ normal(0, 50);

The additive model might really suffer with such wide priors if the
data don't provide much information.


Question: have you tried both the normal and gamma? The nice thing
about Stan is that you can actually build both models and try them out
on your data.


Daniel

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Performance penalty using truncated priors?
parts:
If the normal has a fixed truncation percentage (i.e., it doesn’t depend on parameters), the truncation doesn’t matter in the posterior anyway.  So either choice could work.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Performance penalty using truncated priors?
parts:
We tend to prefer something that focuses the mass
closer to the expected values, but has wide tails, like
a Cauchy. There are now sections in the regression chapter
of the manual with a discussion of recommended priors.

- Bob
